sections.overview: The Barn Swallow is a small, agile passerine that breeds across much of the Northern Hemisphere and moves south when cold weather reduces flying-insect food. Many European populations cross to Africa for winter. Most North American breeders winter in Central or South America. A small breeding population is established in Argentina, well south of the main Northern Hemisphere range. Its use of barns and other buildings brings it close to people, but it remains a wild aerial hunter.
sections.identification: Adults are about 15–18 cm long and weigh roughly 17–20 g; pointed wings and long outer tail feathers give them a swift, deeply forked silhouette. Plumage varies across geographic forms: European birds are relatively pale below, while North American birds are generally darker underneath. Males usually have longer tail streamers than females.
sections.habitat: For breeding, the species needs open airspace rich in flying insects, including meadows, grazed fields, shorelines and wetlands. It commonly attaches a nest to a sheltered beam or ledge in a barn, shed or other outbuilding. Wet mud nearby supplies building material, and shelter helps protect the nest.
sections.diet: Barn Swallows are aerial insectivores: they catch flies, beetles, bees, wasps, ants and moths in flight, often low over grass or water, turning quickly to seize prey. They often select larger individual insects; swallowed grit or tiny shell fragments may help grind food or supply calcium. A farm study linked livestock presence with more large fly and beetle prey in the swallow’s diet.
sections.behavior: The swallow’s agile flight lets it skim over water to drink or bathe without landing. Pairs nest alone or in loose colonies, and migrants gather in communal roosts. Its twittering song and short calls help maintain contact.
sections.reproduction: The pair builds a cup of mud pellets, often mixed with grass and lined with feathers, on a sheltered wall or beam. A typical clutch contains four or five eggs. In Britain, the female usually incubates them for 16–18 days, with occasional help from the male. Chicks hatch altricial, meaning helpless and sparsely feathered, and both parents feed them insects. In Ontario, young fledge at about 19–24 days; parents may continue feeding them for up to a week after they leave the nest.
sections.ecology: By feeding on flying insects, the swallow is both predator and prey: diurnal raptors hunt adults, while rats and squirrels may raid nests in Canada. House Sparrows compete for nest sites and can destroy eggs or chicks; nest parasites can also reduce breeding success.
sections.conservation: Trends vary by region. Canada’s 2021 COSEWIC assessment classed the species as Special Concern, after a Threatened assessment in 2011; national numbers were broadly stable from 2009 to 2019 following a longer decline. Declining insect prey, severe spring temperature swings, agricultural change and some nest-site losses remain concerns, though causes are not fully understood. In the UK, BTO records a 23% breeding-population fall from 1995 to 2024; it also identifies agricultural intensification and winter survival as possible influences.
